subject: Environment
description: Forest types, FSI survey, Forest Policy, forest cover

questions.stem: According to the 'India State of Forest Report' (ISFR) published biennially by the Forest Survey of India, forest cover is defined as all lands of at least 1 hectare with tree-canopy density over:
questions.explanation: FSI defines 'forest cover' as any land > 1 ha with canopy density > 10 % (including orchards, bamboo, palm). Sub-divided into — Very Dense Forest (> 70 %), Moderately Dense (40-70 %), Open Forest (10-40 %). 'Recorded Forest Area' (legal classification under Indian Forest Act) is different and may not coincide with 'forest cover'. As per ISFR 2021, forest cover is ~21.7 % of India's geographical area.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The National Forest Policy of India aims to maintain at least what percentage of the country's geographical area under forest / tree cover?
questions.explanation: National Forest Policy 1988 — 33 % of total geographical area under forest / tree cover overall; 66 % in the hills. Current forest and tree cover together is about 24.6 % (ISFR 2021) — short of the target. The policy's other pillars — meet basic forest needs of tribal / rural poor, conserve biodiversity, control soil erosion, check desertification.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Which Indian state currently has the largest forest cover by area?

options.option_text: Arunachal Pradesh
Madhya Pradesh
Chhattisgarh
Odisha

questions.explanation: MP consistently tops the list by area (~77,000 km²). Arunachal is second by area, Chhattisgarh third, Odisha fourth. In percentage-of-own-area terms, however, the leaders are the NE states — Mizoram (~85 %), Arunachal, Meghalaya. ISFR 2021 data; exact numbers shift slightly every 2 years.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: 'Tropical evergreen' forests in India are found mainly in:

options.option_text: Central Rajasthan
Western Ghats, NE India, Andamans
Deccan plateau
Gangetic plain

questions.explanation: Tropical evergreen forests need > 200 cm annual rainfall + temperature > 22 °C — found in the Western Ghats (Kerala, coastal Karnataka, parts of Maharashtra), NE India (Assam, Arunachal, Meghalaya) and the Andaman-Nicobar islands. Key species — rosewood, mahogany, ebony, rubber. Tropical deciduous ('monsoon') forests are India's most widespread — teak, sal, sandalwood.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The 'Chipko movement' — where villagers hugged trees to prevent them being felled — began in the 1970s in:

options.option_text: Himachal Pradesh
Uttarakhand
Jharkhand
Kerala

questions.explanation: Chipko ('to hug') began in 1973 in Mandal village, Chamoli district, Uttarakhand (then part of UP). Led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Sunderlal Bahuguna, Gaura Devi. The movement's success led to a 15-year ban on commercial felling above 1,000 m in the UP hills (1980). It inspired Appiko (similar tree-hugging movement in Karnataka's Uttara Kannada, 1983).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Sundarbans — the world's largest contiguous mangrove forest — lies in the delta of the:

options.option_text: Mahanadi
Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna
Godavari-Krishna
Narmada-Tapi

questions.explanation: Sundarbans (from 'sundari' tree, Heritiera fomes) — about 10,000 km² across India (West Bengal) and Bangladesh — is the world's largest mangrove forest. Home to the Royal Bengal tiger, estuarine crocodile, Irrawaddy dolphin. UNESCO WHS (1987, Indian part; 1997, Bangladesh part). Mangroves stabilise coasts against storm surges — important natural defence against cyclones.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The Forest Conservation Act, which restricts non-forest use of forest land without Central government approval, was enacted in:
questions.explanation: Forest Conservation Act, 1980 — requires prior Central approval to divert forest land to non-forest use (mining, roads, dams, urban projects). Amended in 2023 (Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam) to ease diversion for certain strategic projects. 1972 — Wildlife Protection Act. 1986 — Environment (Protection) Act. 2006 — Forest Rights Act (giving tribals / forest-dwellers legal rights to forest land and produce).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Van Mahotsav — India's annual week-long tree-plantation festival — was conceived and launched in 1950 by which Union Minister?

options.option_text: Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister
B.R. Ambedkar, chairman of the Drafting Committee
K.M. Munshi, then Union Minister for Agriculture and Food
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, India's Deputy Prime Minister

questions.explanation: K.M. Munshi (also known as 'Kulpati') initiated Van Mahotsav in 1950 while serving as Union Minister for Agriculture and Food, aiming to create public awareness for tree planting. Nehru is a common distractor since he championed many civic campaigns, but the festival's founding is specifically attributed to Munshi.

questions.stem: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 is administered at the Central level by which Ministry?

options.option_text: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Ministry of Tribal Affairs, nodal ministry for this Act
Ministry of Rural Development and Panchayati Raj
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment

questions.explanation: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 is nodally administered by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, not MoEFCC — a distinction frequently tested. MoEFCC handles forest conservation law (Forest Conservation Act), while Tribal Affairs handles community rights within forests. The Act recognises rights of forest-dwelling STs and other traditional forest dwellers.

questions.stem: The 'Arabari experiment' — widely cited as the origin of Joint Forest Management (JFM) in India — was launched in 1972 in which state's Sal forests?

options.option_text: Maharashtra, in the Sahyadri ranges near Pune
Odisha, in the Eastern Ghats tribal belt area
Madhya Pradesh, in the Bastar forest region
West Bengal, in the Midnapore district Sal forests

questions.explanation: Forest officer A.K. Banerjee launched the Arabari experiment in Midnapore (now Paschim Medinipur), West Bengal in 1972, involving local communities in protecting degraded Sal forests in exchange for usufruct rights. It became the model for the national JFM resolution issued by MoEFCC in 1990. Odisha is a tempting distractor because of its large tribal forest belt, but Arabari is firmly in West Bengal.

questions.stem: Which legislation amended the Indian Forest Act, 1927 to exclude bamboo grown outside forest areas from the statutory definition of 'trees', thereby easing livelihood restrictions on farmers and tribal communities?

options.option_text: Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017, passed by Parliament
Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2012, passed by UPA II
Environment Protection (Amendment) Act, 2016, Central Govt
Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022, Parliament

questions.explanation: The Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 redefined the term 'tree' in the parent 1927 Act to remove bamboo grown in non-forest areas from its ambit, so farmers no longer required transit permits to transport bamboo grown on private land. This benefited NE states and tribal farmers considerably. There is no 2012 Indian Forest Amendment — that is a fabricated distractor.

questions.stem: The definitive scientific classification of Indian forests by H.G. Champion and S.K. Seth (revised 1968) organises India's vegetation into how many major forest types?

options.option_text: 8 major groups covering tropical and alpine zones
12 major groups based on rainfall and altitude
16 major groups with 221 distinct minor sub-types
20 major groups including coastal and riverine types

questions.explanation: Champion and Seth (1968) classified Indian forests into 16 major groups and 221 minor types — a figure cited directly in ecology textbooks and UPSC/SSC source material. '12 groups' is a common wrong recall. The classification spans tropical moist evergreen to Alpine forests and remains the standard used by the Forest Survey of India.

questions.stem: Under the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 (CAMPA), what share of the total corpus collected from user agencies is credited to individual State/UT CAMPA funds for ground-level afforestation work?

options.option_text: 90% to states/UTs and 10% retained by the National Fund
60% to states and 40% retained by the National Fund
75% to states and 25% for Central government schemes
50% to states and 50% pooled for inter-state projects

questions.explanation: CAMPA 2016 mandates that 90% of funds flow to State/UT Compensatory Afforestation Funds and only 10% is retained in the National Fund managed by the Central Government. The 90:10 split is specifically designed to ensure afforestation happens where forest land is diverted. Candidates frequently confuse this with a 60:40 or 75:25 split seen in other fiscal-transfer schemes like Finance Commission devolution.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes 'shola' forests, a distinctive forest type frequently mentioned in ecology and environment papers?

options.option_text: Sholas occur above 2,500 m in the Eastern Himalayas with rhododendron
Sholas are restricted to the Nilgiris only, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve
Sholas cover Western Ghats above ~1,500 m; 'shola' derives from Tamil for grove
Sholas are classified as tropical dry deciduous by Champion and Seth

questions.explanation: Shola forests are tropical montane evergreen forests interspersed with rolling grasslands (the 'shola-grassland mosaic') found in the higher elevations of the Western Ghats — Nilgiris, Anamalai, Palani, and Agasthyamalai hills — generally above 1,500 m. The word 'shola' is derived from Tamil 'cholai', meaning a grove or small cluster of trees. Option B is wrong because sholas span multiple hill systems across Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka, not just the Nilgiris. Option D is wrong — they are classified as tropical montane/subtropical hill forests, not dry deciduous.
